title: Chandragupta II
description: Gupta emperor from c. 375 to c. 415
wiki_lead:
Chandragupta II (died c. 415), also known by his title Vikramaditya, as well as Chandragupta Vikramaditya, was the emperor of the Gupta Empire from c. 375 until his death in c. 415. Modern scholars generally identify him with King Chandra of the Delhi iron pillar inscription.
He continued the expansionist policy of his father Samudragupta through military conquests and marital alliances. Historical evidence attests to his remarkable victories, which include the defeat of the Sassanids, the conquest of the Western Kshatrapas and the vassalization of the Hunas. Under the reign of Chandragupta II, the Gupta Empire reached its zenith, directly controlling a vast territory which stretched from the Oxus River in the west to the Bengal region in the east, and from the foothills of the Himalayas in the north to the Narmada River in the south. Chandragupta II expanded his influence and indirectly ruled over the Kuntala region of Karnataka through a marriage alliance with Kadambas, and during his daughter Prabhavatigupta's 20-year-long regency, he effectively integrated the Vakataka dynasty into the Gupta Empire. 
Short Sanskrit inscriptions Found at the Sacred Rock of Hunza in Gilgit-Baltistan mention both Chandra and Harisena. Here Chandra is generally identified as Famous Gupta emperor Chandragupta ІІ and Harisena is identified with Gupta Courtier and minister of his father Emperor Samudragupta. Harisena is not just a Simple poet. The Allahabad Prayaga Prashasti Pillar Identifies him as a Sandhavigrahika(minister of peace and war), Kumaramatya(Senior adminstrative official). This positions shows Harisena held senior administrative position and significant military power under Samudragupta and the Udayagiri Cave Inscriptions demonstrates that experienced ministers could accompany Chandragupta II on royal military expeditions.
Famous Historians such as R.C.Majumdar have explored the possibility and pointed out that the combination of Chandra,Vikramaditya, and mention of Samudragupta's courtier Harisena on the Sacred Rocks of Hunza in Gilgit-Balitstan of Kashmir validates the claim mentioned in the Mehrauli Iron Pillar in Delhi claiming "Chandra" referring to "Chandragupta II Crossing Seven Mouths Of Indus to conquer the Vahlikas". Here the Vahlikas are commonly associated with Bactrian Region Around Balkh in present-day Afghanistan, Although the geographical identification remains debated. This validates the possibility of  Military Expedition conducted by Chandragupta II crossing Indus River and defeating the Vahlikas as claimed in the Chandragupta's Mehrauli Iron Pillar .
Chandragupta II was a devout Vaishnava but tolerated other faiths as well. He was a great patron of learning, and his court is said to have hosted a group of nine scholars known as the Navaratnas (nine gems). His rule strengthened trade, culture, and administration, making him one of India's most celebrated monarchs. The Chinese pilgrim Faxian, who visited India during his reign, suggests that he ruled over a peaceful and prosperous kingdom. The legendary figure of Vikramaditya is probably based on Chandragupta II (among other kings), and the noted Sanskrit poet Kalidasa may have been his court poet. The cave shrines at Udayagiri were also built during his rule. He was succeeded by Kumaragupta I.

Names and titles

Chandragupta II was the second ruler of the dynasty to bear the name "Chandragupta", the first being his grandfather Chandragupta I. He was also simply known as "Chandra", as attested by his coins. The Sanchi inscription of his officer Amrakardava states that he was also known as Deva-raja. The records of his daughter Prabhavatigupta, issued as a Vakataka queen, call him Chandragupta as well as Deva-gupta. Deva-shri (IAST: Devaśri) is another variation of this name. grok_lead: Chandragupta II (c. 375â415 CE), also known by the epithet Vikramaditya, was an emperor of the Gupta dynasty who ruled northern India during the late 4th and early 5th centuries CE, succeeding his father Samudragupta and expanding the empire to its zenith. His reign is marked by military conquests that incorporated western territories, including the defeat of the Western Kshatrapas around 395 CE, granting the Guptas control over Gujarat, Malwa, and access to Arabian Sea ports, as evidenced by the cessation of Saka coinage and the issuance of Gupta dinars in those regions. Under Chandragupta II, the Gupta Empire experienced a flourishing of art, literature, science, and metallurgy, exemplified by inscriptions such as the Mehrauli Iron Pillar dedicated by a king named Chandraâwidely identified as Chandragupta II himselfâto Vishnu, commemorating his victories and showcasing advanced rust-resistant ironwork. His gold coinage, featuring types like the archer and horseman, not only facilitated trade but also propagated imperial iconography, reflecting prosperity and cultural patronage that contributed to the era's designation as India's classical golden age. The association with Vikramaditya, drawn from later traditions and supported by select inscriptions and numismatic evidence, underscores his legendary status as a just and valiant ruler, though primary epigraphic records primarily affirm his territorial and devotional achievements.
